One consults you about comedians, another wishes to recommend
a tragedian; the soothsayer will get varicose veins.
But let her sing rather than go flitting through the whole city,
bold, able to bear the gatherings of men,
and with cloaked generals, in her husband's presence,
to talk herself, with a straight face and dry breasts.
This same woman knows what is happening in all the world, what the Chinese,
what the Thracians are at, the secrets of stepmother
and stepson, who is in love, what adulterer is fought over;
she will tell you who got the widow with child, and in what
month, with what words and in how many ways each woman couples.
She is the first to see the comet that threatens the Armenian
and the Parthian king; she catches the latest news and rumors
at the gates—some she invents: that the Niphates
has burst upon the nations, that there everything is held by a great
flood, that cities are tottering, that lands are sinking;
she tells it at any crossroads to anyone she meets.
Yet that vice is not more intolerable than hers who is wont
to seize her humble neighbors and flog them with thongs,
when begged to do so. For if her deep sleep is broken
by barking, "Bring the cudgels here, quick," she says,
"bring them," and orders the master to be beaten first,
then the dog—grim of approach, most hideous of face.
She goes to the baths by night, has her flasks and her kit moved by
night, loves to sweat in a great uproar;
when her arms have dropped, wearied by the heavy weights,
and the cunning masseur has pressed his fingers on her flesh
and made her thigh's top cry out,
meanwhile her wretched guests are overcome by sleep
and hunger. At last she comes, all flushed, thirsting
for the whole wine-jar, which is set, brimful as an urn,
at her feet, from which a second pint
is drawn before the food, to whet a ravening appetite,
while it comes back up and strikes the ground from her washed-out gut.
The wine runs over the marble; the gilded basin
reeks of Falernian; for she drinks and vomits like a long
snake that has tumbled into a deep vat; and so her husband,
sickened, shuts his eyes and holds back his bile.
But more burdensome still is she who, when she has begun to recline,
praises Virgil, pardons Dido about to die,
pits poets against each other and compares them, hangs Maro
in one scale and Homer in the other.
The grammarians yield, the rhetoricians are beaten, the whole
company falls silent; neither pleader nor crier will speak,
nor any other woman; such a force of words falls down,
you would say so many basins and bells
were being struck at once. Let no one weary the trumpets now, no one the bronze:
she alone will be able to come to the aid of the laboring Moon.
The wise man sets a limit even to honorable things;
for she who longs to seem too learned and eloquent
should hitch her tunic up to mid-thigh,
sacrifice a pig to Silvanus, and bathe for a farthing.
Let not the matron who reclines at your side have
a style of speaking, or whirl a crooked enthymeme in rolling
discourse, or know all the histories,
but let there be some things in books she does not understand. I hate
the woman who is forever poring over and unrolling Palaemon's grammar,
keeping always the law and rule of speech,
and who, an antiquarian, quotes verses unknown to me,
and corrects in a country friend words
no man should care about: let a husband be allowed his solecism.
There is nothing a woman will not permit herself, she thinks nothing shameful,
once she has hung green gems about her neck and fastened
great pearls to her stretched ears;
there is nothing more unbearable than a rich woman.
Meanwhile her face, foul to look at and laughable, swells
with much bread-paste, or breathes out greasy Poppaean ointments,
and on these the lips of her wretched husband stick fast:
to her adulterer she comes with washed skin. When does she care to look
beautiful at home? It is for adulterers that the perfumes are got ready,
for them is bought whatever you slender Indians send us here.
At last she opens her face and lays aside the first coating;
she begins to be recognized, and is soothed with that milk
for which she would lead a herd of she-asses with her
into exile, if she were sent off to the Hyperborean pole.
But she who is plastered over and soothed
with so many medicaments, and takes lumps of boiled
and moistened bread-dough—shall it be called a face, or a sore?
It is worth one's pains to learn thoroughly what they do
and how they spend the whole day. If at night her husband
has lain turned away, the wool-keeper is done for, the dressers
put off their tunics, the litter-bearer is said to have come
late, and is forced to pay the penalty for another's sleep;
this one's rods are broken, that one reddens under the whip,
this one under the lash; some keep torturers on a yearly wage.
She flogs, and meanwhile paints her face, listens to her women friends,
or studies the broad gold of an embroidered robe,
and flogs; she reads across the long day-book
and flogs, until, the floggers worn out, she thunders "Out!"—
dreadful, the inquiry now done.
The governance of her house is no gentler than a Sicilian court;
for if she has fixed it and longs to be adorned more handsomely
than usual, and is in haste, with someone waiting now in the gardens,
or rather at the shrine of the Isiac procuress,
unhappy Psecas, her own hair torn, arranges
her mistress's coiffure, with shoulders and breasts bared.
"Why is this curl too high?" The bull's-hide whip at once
punishes the crime and offense of a misplaced hair.
What has Psecas done? What fault of the girl is it here,
if your own nose has displeased you? Another, on the left,
draws out and combs the locks and rolls them into a circle.
In the council is an old woman, her mother's maid, now retired
from the wool and set over the hairpin; her opinion
will be first; after her, those lesser in age and skill
will vote, as if reputation or life
were at stake: so great is the care of seeking beauty;
with so many tiers she presses, with so many courses she builds up
her lofty head; you will see an Andromache in front;
behind she is smaller—you would think her another woman. Suppose she has been allotted
a short span of little stature, and looks shorter
than a Pygmy maiden, helped by no high heels,
and rises lightly on tiptoe to a kiss.
Meanwhile no care is taken for the husband, no mention is made
of his losses. She lives as if she were her husband's neighbor,
closer only in this—that she hates his friends
and his slaves, and is a burden on his accounts. Look, the chorus
of frenzied Bellona and the Mother of the gods enters, and a huge
half-man, a face the lesser obscene crew must revere,
who long ago cut off his soft genitals with a broken sherd,
before whom the hoarse troop, before whom the timbrels give way;
his common cheeks are wrapped in a Phrygian tiara.
He bawls aloud and bids her dread the coming of September
and the South Wind, unless she purifies herself with a hundred eggs
and presents him with her old dark-red gowns,
so that whatever sudden and great peril threatens
may pass into the garments and atone for the whole year at once.
In winter she will go down into the river through broken ice,
plunge three times in the morning Tiber,
and wash her timid head in the very eddies; then over the whole field
of the proud king she will creep, naked and trembling, on bleeding
knees; if white Io commands, she will go
to the end of Egypt and fetch waters sought
from warm Meroe, to sprinkle them in the temple
of Isis, which rises next to the ancient sheepfold.
For she believes she is warned by the very voice of the mistress goddess:
behold a soul and mind with which the gods may talk at night!
So the chief and highest honor is earned by him
who, ringed with a linen-clad troop and a bald-headed troop,
runs as Anubis, mocking the wailing people.
He begs forgiveness whenever a wife does not abstain
from intercourse on the holy and to-be-observed days,
and a great penalty is owed for the violated coverlet,
and the silver serpent was seen to move its head;
his tears and his studied mutterings procure
that Osiris will not refuse pardon for the fault—
bribed, of course, by a fat goose and a thin cake.
When he has given place, a quaking Jewess, leaving her basket
and her hay behind, begs at her secret ear,
interpreter of the laws of Jerusalem and high priestess
of the tree and trusty go-between of highest heaven.
She too fills her hand, but more sparingly; for a small coin
the Jews will sell you dreams of any sort you please.
A tender lover, or the huge legacy of a rich
childless man, an Armenian or Commagenian soothsayer
promises, after handling the lung of a warm dove;
he will probe the breasts of chickens, the entrails of a puppy,
sometimes even of a boy; he will do what he can then inform upon.
But in the Chaldeans there will be greater trust: whatever
the astrologer says, they will believe brought back from the spring
of Ammon, since the oracles at Delphi have ceased
and the darkness of the future condemns the human race.
Yet the chief of these is one who has often been an exile,
through whose friendship—if his right hand has clanked with iron
and his left, if he has long dwelt in a camp-prison—
the trust in his art comes. No astrologer will have genius
if he is uncondemned, but one who has barely escaped, who has just managed
to be sent to a Cyclad, and at last to be quit of little Seriphos.
She consults him about the lingering death of her jaundiced mother,
but first, your Tanaquil, about you—when she will bury
her sister and her uncles, whether her adulterer will outlive
her own self: for what greater thing can the gods grant?
Yet this woman does not know what the grim star
of Saturn threatens, under what constellation Venus shows herself glad,
which months are for losses, what seasons are given for gain:
remember to avoid even the meeting of her
in whose hands you see, like fat amber, well-thumbed
almanacs; she who consults no one and is now
consulted herself, who, when her husband seeks the camp or his country,
will not go with him, called back by the calculations of Thrasyllus.
When she chooses to be carried to the first milestone, the hour
is taken from a book; if the rubbed corner of her eye
itches, she asks for salve only after her horoscope is inspected;
though she lies sick, no hour seems fitter
for taking food than the one Petosiris has appointed.
If she is of middling rank, she will pace the space on each side
of the race-course turning-posts and draw lots, and offer her forehead
and her hand to the seer who asks for repeated lip-smackings.
To the rich a Phrygian augur will give responses, or a hired
Indian; one skilled in the stars and the sky will give them,
and some old man who buries the public lightning-bolts:
the plebeian's fate is set in the circus and on the embankment.
She who displays a long gold chain on her bare neck
consults, before the scaffolds and the dolphin-columns,
whether to leave the tavern-keeper and marry the cloak-seller.
Yet these women undergo the perils of childbirth and endure
all the labors of nursing, as their lot constrains them;
but scarcely any lies in childbed in a gilded couch,
so great is the power of that woman's arts, her drugs,
who makes women barren and hires herself out to kill
men in the womb. Rejoice, you wretch, and hold out yourself
whatever it is to be drunk; for if she chose to swell
and trouble her belly with leaping babies, you might perhaps
become the father of an Ethiopian—soon a dark heir
would fill your will, one you would never wish to see at dawn.
I pass over the foundlings, the joys and prayers so often
deceived at the foul cisterns, and the pontiffs
fetched from there, and the Salii destined to bear the names
of the Scauri in a false body. Wicked Fortune stands by night,
smiling on the naked infants; these she cherishes and folds
in her whole bosom, then hands them up to lofty houses,
preparing for herself a private farce; these she loves, on these
she presses herself, and forever brings them forward as her foster-children.
This man brings magic spells, this one sells Thessalian
philters, by which she may have power to trouble her husband's mind
and to thrash his buttocks with her slipper: it is from these
that your wits are gone, from these the darkness of your mind and the great
forgetting of the things you did but now. Yet this is bearable, if
you do not also begin to rave, like that uncle of Nero,
into whose whole forehead Caesonia poured
the fluid of a trembling foal's brow. What will the wife of an emperor not do?
Everything was ablaze and falling in with its frame shattered,
just as if Juno had made her husband mad;
less harmful, then, will Agrippina's mushroom be,
since it pressed the heart of one old man alone
and bade his palsied head go down
into heaven, his lips streaming with long slaver;
but this potion demands sword and fire, this one racks,
this tears apart the senators mixed with the blood of knights.
So much does a single poisoner cost; so much the foal of a mare.
They hate the children of a mistress: let no one resist,
let no one forbid; now, now it is lawful to kill a stepson.
You wards, I warn you, whose estate is the greater,
guard your lives and trust no dish:
those rich pastries reek, livid with a mother's poison.
Let someone bite first whatever she hands you
who bore you; let your timid tutor taste the cups before you.
Now all this, of course, is our invention; satire is putting on
the lofty buskin, and, overstepping the bounds and law of our forebears,
we rave a grand song in the Sophoclean gape,
a thing unknown to the Rutulian hills and the Latin sky?
Would that we were idle dreamers! But Pontia cries, "I did it,
I confess, and I prepared the aconite for my own children,
which, discovered, lies open; yet I myself carried out the deed."
"You—two, at one supper, you most savage viper?"
"You—two?" "Seven, had there happened to be seven!"
Let us believe whatever the tragedians say of the grim
Colchian and of Procne; I make no objection. They too
dared great monstrous deeds in their day, but
not for the sake of money; less wonder is owed
to the greatest monstrosities, whenever anger drives this sex
into guilt, and, with frenzy firing the liver, they are carried
headlong, like rocks torn from a ridge, from which the mountain
is drawn away and the hanging slope falls back.
That woman I could not endure who reckons it up and, cool-headed,
commits a monstrous crime. They watch Alcestis going
under her husband's fate, and, were a like exchange offered,
would gladly save a lapdog's life by their husband's death.
You will meet many a daughter of Belus and Eriphyle
in the morning; not a street but will have its Clytemnestra.
This much only is the difference—that the famed daughter of Tyndareus
held a clumsy, witless axe in right hand and left,
but now the deed is done with the thin lung of a toad;
yet with steel too, if her Atrides has cautiously
forearmed himself with the Pontic remedies of the thrice-conquered king."
Satire VII All the hope and reason of learning rests on Caesar alone;
for he alone in this age has looked with favor on the sad Muses,
when poets now famous and well known
were trying to take a little bath-house at Gabii, or ovens at Rome,
and others thought it neither foul nor shameful
to become auctioneers, when hungry Clio,
her Aganippean valleys deserted, migrated into the salerooms.
For if not one farthing is shown to you in the Pierian
shade, you might come to love the name and livelihood of Machaera
and sell instead, as the auctioneer sells to the bystanders
what is put in his charge—a wine-jar, tripods, cabinets, chests,
the Alcithoe of Pacuvius, the Thebes and Tereus of Faustus.
This is better than to say before a judge, "I saw"
what you did not see—let the Asian knights do that,
and the Cappadocians, whom the other Gaul brands on their bare ankle.
Yet no one henceforth will be forced to bear toil
unworthy of his studies, whoever weaves vocal
eloquence into tuneful measures, and has bitten the laurel.
Set to it, young men: the indulgence of our leader watches over you,
and spurs you on, and seeks out matter for itself.
If you think any other support for your affairs
is to be looked for elsewhere, and so the parchment of the saffron
tablet is filled up—be quick, ask for some firewood, and the verses
you compose, Telesinus, give to Venus' husband,
or shut them away and let the bookworm bore through the shelved volumes;
break your pen, poor wretch, and blot out the battles you sat up to write,
you who make sublime poems in a cramped little cell,
that you may come out worthy of the ivy and a lean bust.
There is no hope beyond. The rich miser has now learned
only to admire, only to praise the eloquent,
as boys do Juno's bird. But the time of life slips away
that can endure the sea and the helmet and the mattock.
Then weariness creeps over the spirit, then eloquent
and naked old age hates itself and its own Terpsichore.
Now hear the tricks, so that the man may give you nothing—
the man you cultivate, having quit the temple of the Muses and Apollo.
He himself writes verses, and yields only to Homer
on account of his thousand years; and if, fired by the sweetness
of fame, you give a reading, he lends you a dingy hall;
this house, far off and iron-barred, is set to serve you,
a house whose door mimics anxious city-gates.
He knows how to post freedmen seated in the farthest part
of the row, and to arrange the loud voices of his clients:
none of these great men will give what the benches cost,
and the tiers that hang from a hired beam,
and the orchestra set out with chairs to be carried back.
Yet we keep at this, and draw furrows in the thin
dust, and turn the shore with a barren plow.
For if you try to break away, the noose of the ambitious
itch for writing holds you, and grows old in your sick heart.
But the poet of distinction, who has no common vein,
who is not wont to spin out anything trite, nor
to strike a vulgar song from common coin—
such a one, whom I cannot point out and only feel,
is made by a mind free from anxiety, impatient of all
bitterness, eager for the woods, and fit to drink
the springs of the Aonides. For poverty cannot sing
in the Pierian grotto or touch the thyrsus, when it is
cast down and bare of the coin which night and day
the body needs: Horace is well fed when he cries "Euhoe!"
What room is there for genius, unless when your hearts,
vexed by song alone and swept away by the lords of Cirrha and Nysa,
admit no two cares at once?
It is the work of a great mind, not one struck dumb by the thought
of buying a blanket, to gaze on chariots and horses and the faces
of gods, and on the sort of Fury that confounds the Rutulian.
For if Virgil had lacked a slave-boy and a tolerable
lodging, all the snakes would have fallen from the Fury's hair,
the muffled trumpet would have groaned nothing deep: do we ask that
Rubrenus Lappa be no less than the ancient buskin,
he who pawns his bowls and his cloak to write his Atreus?
Unhappy Numitor has nothing to send a friend:
he has something to give Quintilla, nor did he lack
the means to buy a lion to be fattened on much flesh,
already tamed; no doubt the beast costs less to keep—
a poet's guts, of course, take more.
Let Lucan lie content with fame in his marble
gardens; but for Serranus and slender Saleius,
what is glory, however great, if it is glory only?
Men run to the sweet voice and song of the beloved
Thebaid, when Statius has gladdened the city
and named the day: with such sweetness he affects
the captive souls, and with such delight he is heard
by the crowd; but when he has shattered the benches with his verse,
he goes hungry, unless he sells his virgin Agave to Paris.
That man bestows on many the honor of military rank,
and rings poets' fingers with the gold of a six-month tribuneship:
what the nobles do not give, an actor will. Do you court
the Camerini and a Barea, the great halls of the nobility?
Pelopea makes prefects, Philomela tribunes.
Yet you need not envy the poet whom the stage feeds:
who will be your Maecenas now, who Proculeius
or Fabius? Who another Cotta, who a second Lentulus?
Then the reward matched the talent, then it profited many
to grow pale and to drink no wine the whole of December.
Moreover, is your labor more fruitful, you writers
of history? More time perishes here, and more oil.
For the thousandth page, knowing no limit, rises
for each of you, and the costly heap of papyrus grows;
the vast number of facts demands it, and the law of the work.
Yet what harvest comes from it? What fruit of the broken ground?
Who will give a historian as much as he would a clerk reading the gazette?
"But they are a lazy breed, fond of the couch and the shade."
Tell me, then, what civic duties profit the pleaders,
and the briefs that go along in a great bundle.
They sound off grandly themselves, but chiefly when a creditor
is listening, or if someone keener than he has touched their side—
a man who comes about a doubtful debt with a great ledger.
Then the empty bellows breathe out vast lies,
and the front of the toga is spat upon: if you care to grasp
the real harvest, set on this side the estates of a hundred pleaders,
on the other put alone the wealth of Lacerta, the Red charioteer.
The chiefs have taken their seats; you rise, a pale Ajax,
to plead for doubtful liberty before a cowherd
for judge. Burst your strained liver, poor wretch, so that, worn out,
the green palms, the glory of your staircase, may be set up for you.
And what is the price of your voice? A dry little ham, and a jar
of sprats, or some old onions, the monthly ration of the Moors,
or wine carried down the Tiber—five flagons.
If you have pleaded four times, if one gold piece has come your way,
from that the agents' shares fall due by agreement.
To Aemilius will be given as much as the law allows, though we
pleaded better; for his bronze chariot stands, with tall
four-horse teams, in his hall, and he himself, seated
on a fierce war-horse, threatens with a curved spear from afar,
and rehearses battles with his one-eyed statue.
So Pedo goes bankrupt, Matho fails; this is the end
of Tongilius, who is wont to bathe with a great rhinoceros-horn flask
and to plague the baths with his muddy throng,
and presses the young Maedians through the forum with his long pole-borne litter,
about to buy boys, silver, murrhine, villas;
for his ship-borne purple, with its Tyrian thread, stands surety.
And yet this pays them: purple sells
the pleader, the amethyst-dyed cloaks sell him; it suits him
to live with the noise and the show of a greater fortune.
But spendthrift Rome keeps no limit to expense.
Do we trust to eloquence? No one would now give Cicero
two hundred coins, unless a great ring flashed.
The man who goes to law looks first at this: whether you have
eight slaves, ten companions, a sedan behind you, men in togas
before your feet. And so Paulus pleaded in a hired
sardonyx, and so charged more than Gallus,
than Basilus. Eloquence is rare in a threadbare cloak.
When is Basilus allowed to bring forward a weeping mother?
Who could bear Basilus, though he speak well? Let Gaul take you,
or rather Africa, the nursemaid of pleaders,
if you have resolved to set a price on your tongue.
Do you teach declamation? O iron heart of Vettius,
when his numerous class destroys cruel tyrants!
For whatever he has just read sitting down, the same he will deliver
standing, and will chant the same in the same verses;
the cabbage served up again kills the wretched masters.
What the color, what the kind of case, where the chief
question lies, what arrows may come from the opposing side—
all wish to know, no one to pay the fee.
"The fee, you say?" "Why, what do I know?" The teacher's fault,
of course, is blamed, that in the left side of his breast
nothing throbs for the Arcadian youth, who every sixth
day fills my wretched head with his dreadful Hannibal,
whatever it is he is debating: whether to march on Rome
from Cannae, or, after the storms and lightning, cautiously
wheel back his cohorts, soaked by the tempest.
Bargain for any sum you please, and take it down at once: what would I give
to have the father hear him as often as I do? These six others,
or more, all clamor with one mouth, the sophists,
and plead real cases, the abductor abandoned;
the poisonings fall silent, the wicked and ungrateful husband,
and the mortars that now cure the old and blind.
So he will give himself his own discharge, if he heeds
our counsel, and will enter on a different path of life,
the man who has come down from the rhetorician's shade to the fight,
lest the little sum perish for which a cheap ticket of grain
is bought; for this is the choicest of wages. Try
how much Chrysogonus, how much Pollio charges to teach
the children of the rich: you will tear up Theodorus' treatise.
Baths cost six hundred thousand, and more the colonnade in which
the master is carried whenever it rains—is he to wait for fair weather,
or splatter his beasts with fresh mud?
Here rather, for here the hoof of the clean mule shines.
In another part let a dining-hall, propped on tall
Numidian columns, rise and catch the cold sun.
Whatever the house, there will come one to set out the courses
skillfully, one to season the relishes.
Among such expenses, two thousand sesterces for Quintilian
would be plenty; nothing will cost a father less
than his son. "Whence then has Quintilian
so many estates?" Pass over the examples of new
fortunes: lucky, handsome, and keen,
lucky, wise, noble, and well-born,
the lucky man stitches the crescent to his black shoe;
lucky too the greatest orator and javelin-thrower,
and, even if he has caught a chill, he sings well. For it makes a difference
what stars receive you, just as you begin to utter your first
cries, still red from your mother.
If Fortune wills, you will become a consul out of a rhetor;
if this same Fortune wills, a rhetor out of a consul.
For what was Ventidius? What Tullius? Anything but
a star and the marvelous power of hidden fate?
Fate gives kingdoms to slaves, a triumph to captives.
Yet that lucky man is rarer even than a white crow.
Many have repented of the empty and barren chair,
as the end of Thrasymachus proves, and of Secundus
Carrinas; and you, Athens, saw him poor,
having dared to bestow on him nothing but cold hemlock.
May the gods grant our forefathers' shades light, weightless earth
and breathing crocuses and an everlasting spring in the urn,
who decreed that a teacher should hold the place
of a revered parent. Achilles, now grown great, in dread of the rod
would sing in his native hills, and even then the tail
of his lyre-master could draw a laugh from no one;
but his own pupils flog Rufus and the rest, each man his own—
Rufus, whom he so often called the Allobrogian Cicero.
Who pays into the lap of Celadus or learned Palaemon
as much as the grammarian's toil has earned? And yet out of this,
whatever it is—and it is less than the rhetor's fee—
the boy's escort, the boorish guardian, takes a first bite,
and the steward breaks off something for himself. Give way, Palaemon,
and bear with some shrinkage from it, just as
the peddler of a winter mat and snowy blanket does,
provided only that nothing be lost of what, from the midnight hour,
you sat for, when no workman, when no one would sit
who teaches to draw out wool with the slanting iron;
provided only that nothing be lost of having smelled as many lamps
as there stood boys, while Flaccus grew quite discolored
and the soot clung to a blackened Maro.
Yet the fee is rare that does not need the tribunal's
cognizance. But you, impose your savage laws,
that the rule of words hold good for the teacher,
that he read the histories, know all the authors
as well as his own nails and fingers, so that, asked by chance
while going to the warm baths or the baths of Phoebus, he may tell
the nurse of Anchises, the name and country of the stepmother
of Anchemolus, may say how many years Acestes lived,
how many jars of Sicilian wine he gave the Phrygians;
require that he mold tender characters as with the thumb,
as one shapes a face in wax; require that he be
even the father of the company himself, lest they play foul games,
lest they do shameful things by turns; it is no light task
to watch the hands and the trembling eyes of so many boys.
"This," he says, "is your charge; but when the year has come round,
receive the gold the people demand for a victor."
Satire VIII What do pedigrees avail? What use is it, Ponticus, to be reckoned
by long descent, to show the painted faces
of ancestors, the Aemiliani standing in their chariots,
and the Curii now but halves, a Corvinus reduced to a shoulder,
and a Galba lacking ears and nose?
What profit to flaunt on the spreading family-tree
a Corvinus, and thereafter to touch with many a branch
the smoke-stained masters of the horse along with a dictator,
if you live basely before the Lepidi? To what end so many
images of warriors, if the dice are played all night
before the Numantini, if you begin to sleep at the rising
of the morning star, when the generals were moving their standards and camp?
Why should a Fabius, born in the household of Hercules, rejoice
in the title "Allobrogicus" and the Great Altar, if he is greedy, if
vain, and softer than any Euganean lamb,
if, his tender loin smoothed with Catanian pumice,
he disgraces his rough ancestors, and—a buyer of poison—
dishonors his wretched line with an image that must be broken?
Though ancient waxen busts adorn your halls on every side,
nobility is the one and only virtue.
Be a Paulus or a Cossus or a Drusus in your morals;
set these before the images of your ancestors,
let them go before the very rods when you are consul.
You owe me first the goods of the soul. Do you earn to be held holy
and steadfast in justice in deed and word?
I recognize a noble: hail, Gaetulicus, or you,
Silanus, of whatever other blood, a rare
and excellent citizen, you fall to your rejoicing country—
one is moved to cry out what the people cry when Osiris
is found. For who would call him noble who is
unworthy of his line and distinguished only
by an illustrious name? We call some man's dwarf an Atlas,
an Ethiopian a Swan, a crooked, deformed girl
a Europa; lazy curs, smooth with old mange,
and licking the rim of a dry lamp,
will be named Panther, Tiger, Lion, or whatever else there is
that roars more fiercely on the earth; so you will beware
and fear lest you be a "Creticus" or "Camerinus" in that fashion.
Whom have I warned by this? With you is my discourse, Rubellius
Blandus. You swell with the high pedigree of the Drusi, as though
you had yourself done something to make you noble,
something to make her who shines with the blood of Iulus conceive you,
not the woman hired to weave beneath the windy embankment.
"You are low," you say, "the very dregs of our rabble,
none of whom could point to his father's birthplace;
but I am a son of Cecrops." Long life to you, and may you
bear long the joys of this origin: yet from the lowest commons
you will find an eloquent Roman; this man is wont to defend the cases
of an unlettered noble; from the toga-clad plebs will come
one to untie the knots of the law and the riddles of statutes;
from here a young man, busy in arms, makes for the Euphrates
and the eagles that guard the conquered Batavian. But you
are nothing but a son of Cecrops, most like a headless Herm:
for there is no other difference between you, except that
his head is of marble, and your image lives.
Tell me, offspring of the Teucri: who would think dumb
animals well-bred, unless they are strong? It is for this, surely,
that we praise the swift horse, for whom many a palm
burns easily and victory exults in the hoarse circus;
that one is noble, from whatever pasture he comes, whose
flight is glorious before the rest and who is first to raise the dust on the course;
but the offspring of Coryphaeus and Hirpinus are a salable herd,
if victory has rarely settled on their yoke;
there is no regard there for ancestors, no favor
for the shades; they are bidden to change masters for a paltry
price, and, slow-footed, with worn-down neck, drag the cart,
grandsons fit to turn the mill.
So, that we may admire you and not your forebears, give us something of your own,
something I may carve on your titles besides the honors
we give and have given to those to whom you owe everything.
This is enough for the youth whom rumor hands down to us as proud
and puffed up and full of his kinsman Nero;
for common sense is generally rare in that
high fortune. But I would not have you, Ponticus,
valued by the praise of your forebears in such a way that you yourself do nothing
for future glory. It is wretched to lean on the fame of others,
lest, the columns withdrawn, the roof come crashing down.
The vine-shoot stretched on the ground longs for its widowed elms.
Be a good soldier, a good guardian, an upright
arbiter too; if ever you are summoned as witness
in a doubtful and uncertain case, though Phalaris command you to be
false and dictate perjury with his bull brought near,
believe it the greatest sin to prefer life to honor,
and, for the sake of living, to lose the grounds of living.
He who deserves death has perished, though he dine on a hundred oysters
from the Gauran rock and bathe in a whole cauldron of Cosmus' scent.
When the long-awaited province at last receives you
as its governor, set a curb and a limit to your anger,
set one to your greed as well; pity the needy allies:
you see the bones of their realm, sucked dry of marrow;
mark what the laws advise, what the senate enjoins,
what great rewards await the good, with what just thunderbolt
both Capito and Numitor fell, the senate condemning them,
pirates of the Cilicians. But what does a sentence avail?
Look for an auctioneer, Chaerippus, for your rags,
since Pansa snatches whatever Natta left you;
and now be silent: it is madness, after losing all, to lose the fare too.
The groan was not the same in old days, nor was the wound equal,
when our allies' losses were fresh and they but lately conquered.
Every house was then full, and a great heap
of coins stood there, a Spartan cloak, Coan purples,
and along with the paintings of Parrhasius and the statues of Myron,
the ivory of Phidias was alive, nor was the much
labor of Polyclitus lacking anywhere, and rare were the tables without a Mentor.
From there Dolabella, from there Antonius, from there
sacrilegious Verres carried back in their tall ships
hidden spoils, and more triumphs over peace than over war.
Now from the allies a few yoke of oxen, a small herd of mares,
and the father of the flock will be snatched from a captured little field,
then the household gods themselves, if there is any notable statue,
if any single god in his little shrine; for these indeed are now
their greatest things, these are now their utmost. You might perhaps
despise the unwarlike Rhodians and oiled Corinth;
and despise them with reason: what will the resined youths
and the smooth legs of a whole nation do to you?
But shun rough Spain, the Gallic clime,
and the Illyrian coast; spare too those harvesters
who fill the city that has leisure for the circus and the stage.
And what reward will you bring from there for so dire a crime,
now that Marius has lately stripped the impoverished Africans?
Above all take care that no great wrong be done
to the brave and the wretched: though you take away all the gold
and silver there is anywhere, you will leave them shield and sword.
What I have just set down is no mere maxim: it is truth—
believe that I recite to you a leaf of the Sibyl.
If your band of companions is holy, if no long-haired page
sells your tribunal, if there is no fault in your wife,
nor any Harpy ready to go through the assizes and all the towns
with hooked talons to snatch your money,
then you may count your descent from Picus, and if lofty
names delight you, set among your forebears the whole
Titanian war and Prometheus himself,
take your great-grandsire from whatever book you please.
But if ambition and lust drag you headlong,
if you break your rods in the blood of the allies, if you delight
in blunted axes and a weary lictor,
then the very nobility of your own ancestors begins
to stand against you, and to hold a bright torch before your shameful deeds.
Every fault of the soul carries the more conspicuous
guilt the greater the man who sins is held to be.
To what end do you tell me of your wont to seal false tablets
in the temples your grandfather built, and before your father's
triumphal statue? To what end, if a nocturnal adulterer,
you veil your muffled temples in a Santonic hood?
Past the ashes and bones of his ancestors, in a flying
carriage, fat Lateranus is whirled, and he himself,
the consul-muleteer, locks the wheel with his own brake.
By night, indeed, but the Moon sees, but the stars as witnesses
strain their eyes. When his term of office is ended,
Lateranus will take up his whip in broad daylight,
and will not blush to meet a friend
now old, and will salute him first with his wand, and will untie
the hay-bundles and pour out the barley for his weary beasts.
Meanwhile, while he slaughters the woolly victims and the russet bullock
in Numa's fashion, he swears before Jupiter's altars
by Epona alone and the faces painted on the rank stalls.
But when he chooses to revisit the all-night taverns,
a Syrophoenician, greasy with constant balsam, runs to meet him,
a Syrophoenician dwelling at the Idumaean gate,
and with a host's affection greets him as lord and king,
and Cyane too, girt up, with her wine-jar for sale.
The defender of the fault will say to me: "We did
these things too, as young men." Granted; you stopped, of course, nor
beyond that did you nurse the error: let your shameful daring be brief.
Some faults should be cut off with the first beard;
grant pardon to boys: but Lateranus goes to those
bath-house cups and inscribed napkins
ripe for the war of defending the rivers of Armenia and Syria,
and the Rhine and the Danube; this age is fit to keep
Nero secure. Send to Ostia, Caesar,
send—but seek your legate in a great cookshop;
you will find him lying with some cutthroat,
mixed in with sailors and thieves and runaways,
among hangmen and coffin-makers
and the silent timbrels of a sprawled-out priest of Cybele.
There is equal liberty there, shared cups, a couch
no different for anyone, a table set no farther off for any.
What would you do, Ponticus, if you got such a slave?
You would send him, surely, to the Lucanians or a Tuscan workhouse.
But you, sons of Troy, forgive yourselves, and what is shameful
in a cobbler will befit a Volesus or a Brutus.
What if we never use examples so foul
and so shameful that worse do not remain?
Your wealth consumed, Damasippus, you hired your voice
to the curtain, to play the noisy Ghost of Catullus.
Nimble Lentulus too acted Laureolus well,
worthy in my judgment of a real cross; nor would I pardon
the people itself: the brow of this people is too hard,
which sits and watches the buffooneries of patricians,
hears the barefoot Fabii, can laugh at
the slaps of the Mamerci. At what price they sell their deaths,
what does it matter? They sell with no Nero compelling them,
nor do they hesitate to sell themselves at the lofty praetor's games.
Yet suppose swords were set on one side and stages on the other,
which is better? Has anyone so shuddered at death
as to be the jealous husband of Thymele, the colleague of dull Corinthus?
It is no great wonder, though, that, with a lyre-player for emperor,
a noble plays the mime. Beyond this, what is there but the arena? And there
you have the city's disgrace: not a Gracchus fighting in a murmillo's
arms, nor with shield, nor with a trident leveled;
for he condemns such garb—condemns it and hates it;
nor does a helmet hide his face. Look, he wields the trident.
After he has cast, with hand quivering, the dangling nets
in vain, he lifts his bare face to the spectators
and flees, to be recognized over the whole arena.
Let us believe the tunic, when the gold cord
stretches from his throat and the spiral tosses from his long cap.
So the pursuer, ordered to fight with the Gracchus, bore a disgrace
heavier than any wound.
If free votes were given to the people, who would be so
abandoned as to hesitate to prefer Seneca to Nero?
For whose punishment one ape should not have been provided,
nor one serpent, nor one sack.
Equal was the crime of Agamemnon's son, but the cause makes
the matter unlike: for he, with the gods to authorize it, avenged
his father slain amid the cups; but he did not
defile himself with Electra's throat, nor Sparta
with the blood of a wife, mixed aconite for no kinsmen,
never sang Orestes on the stage,
wrote no Trojan poem. For what should Verginius rather
have avenged with arms, or Galba with Vindex,
than the deeds Nero did in his savage and cruel tyranny?
These are the works and these the arts of a high-born prince,
who delighted to prostitute himself with foul song on foreign stages
and to earn the parsley of a Greek garland.
Let your ancestors' images have the insignia of your voice;
before Domitius' feet set down the long train
of Thyestes, or of Antigone, or the mask of Melanippe,
and hang your lyre from your marble colossus.
What, Catiline, will anyone find loftier than your birth
and Cethegus'? Yet you prepare nocturnal arms
and flames for houses and temples,
like the sons of the trousered ones and the descendants of the Senones,
daring what may be punished with the painful tunic.
But the consul is awake and curbs your standards;
this new man from Arpinum, low-born and but lately
a municipal knight at Rome, posts a helmeted
guard everywhere for the terrified, and toils on every hill.
So within the walls the toga won for him as much
as Octavius took on the fields of Leucas and Thessaly
with a sword wet from constant slaughter; but Rome, while free,
called Cicero parent, Rome called him father of his country.
Another man of Arpinum was wont, on the Volscian hills,
to ask his wages, weary of another's plow;
after that he would break the knotty vine-staff on his head,
if he were slow in fortifying the camp with a sluggish mattock;
yet this man meets the Cimbri and the utmost perils of the state,
and alone protects the trembling city.
And so, after the ravens, which had never lit on greater corpses,
flew to the Cimbri and the slaughter,
his noble colleague is honored with a second laurel.
Plebeian were the souls of the Decii, plebeian their names;
yet these sufficed, for whole legions and for
all the auxiliaries and the whole Latin youth,
to the gods below and Mother Earth;
for the Decii were worth more than what they saved.
Born of a slave-woman, the last of the good kings earned
the royal robe and diadem of Quirinus and the rods.
The consul's own sons were loosing the bolts of the gates,
betrayed, to the exiled tyrants, sons who ought to have dared
something great for liberty in its peril,
something Mucius might marvel at, with Cocles, and the maid
who swam the Tiber, the boundary of empire:
a slave brought the hidden crimes to the senators—
a slave to be mourned by matrons; but them the lash
afflicts with just penalties, and the first axe of the laws.
I would rather you had Thersites for a father, provided you were
like the grandson of Aeacus and could wield the arms of Vulcan,
than that Achilles should beget you like Thersites.
And yet, however far back you trace, however far you unroll
the name, you draw your line from an infamous sanctuary:
the first of your ancestors, whoever he was,
was either a shepherd or that which I would rather not say.
Satire IX I should like to know, Naevolus, why so often you meet me
downcast, your brow clouded like Marsyas defeated.
What have you to do with the look that Ravola wore when he was caught,
while he rubbed Rhodope's privates with his wet beard?
We give a cuff to a slave who licks the pastries.
Crepereius Pollio will have no more pitiable a face than this,
who, ready to pay triple interest, goes round
and finds no fools. Whence, all at once,
so many wrinkles? Surely you used to play, content with little,
the homebred knight, a guest with a biting jest,
vehement with the wit and salt born within the city bounds.
Now everything is the reverse: a grave face, a rough, dry
thicket of hair, no gloss at all on your whole skin, such as
the Bruttian gum of warm bird-lime once gave you,
but your legs neglected and squalid with sprouting hair.
What of this leanness, like that of an old sick man whom for a long time
the quartan fever roasts, and the once-domestic ague?
You may detect the torments of a soul hidden in a sick
body; you may detect its joys too; the face takes
both habits from within; so you seem to have turned
your purpose and to be going against your former life.
For lately, as I recall, the shrine of Isis and the Ganymede
of Peace, and the secret Palatine of the imported Mother,
and Ceres (for in what temple does no woman stand for sale?),
you were wont to haunt, an adulterer more notorious than Aufidius,
and—what you keep silent—to bend over the very husbands too.
"This way of life is profitable to many, but to me no
reward of my labor has come of it: now and then some greasy cloaks,
the toga's defenses, of a hard and coarse color
and badly beaten by the comb of a Gallic weaver,
a thin bit of silver, of the second vein.
Fate rules men, fate governs even those parts
which the garment hides; for if your stars fail you,
the unmeasured length of your member will avail you nothing,
though Virro see you naked with foaming lip,
and coaxing notes, thick and unceasing,
solicit you—for of himself a deviant draws a man on.
Yet what monster is worse than a stingy lecher?
'I gave you this, then I gave you that, soon you got more':
he reckons it up, and wags his rump. Let the counter be set out, let the boys
be at hand with the slate; count up five thousand sesterces
for all my services: then let my labors be counted too.
Is it easy and downhill work to drive a proper member
into the bowels, and there to meet yesterday's dinner?
The slave who has dug a field will be less wretched
than he who digs his master. But you, of course, thought yourself
a tender boy, and fair, and worthy of the cup and of heaven.
Will you, you patrons, you, ever indulge a humble hanger-on,
a faithful worshipper, now that you are not even ready to give for the disease?
There's the man for whom you should send a green parasol, for whom
great pieces of amber, whenever his birthday returns or the moist spring
begins, and, laid out on his cushioned, long chair,
he handles in secret the gifts of the women's Kalends.
Tell me, you sparrow, for whom do you keep so many hills, so many Apulian
estates, so many kites grown weary within your pastures?
The Trifoline land stocks you with fertile vines,
and the ridge that looks down on Cumae, and empty Gaurus—
for who coats more jars with must that will last?—
how much would it have cost to give your exhausted client's loins
a few acres? Is it better that this country infant,
with his mother and his cottage and his playmate puppy,
be left as a legacy to the friend who beats the cymbals?
'You are shameless to ask,' he says. But the rent cries out 'Ask';
and so does my one slave, like the broad eye of Polyphemus
by which clever Ulysses made his escape.
A second must be bought, for this one is not enough; both
must be fed. What shall I do when the winter wind blows? What, pray,
what shall I say to my boys' shoulders and feet
in the December north-wind? 'Hold out, and wait for the cicadas'?
But, however you dissemble it, though you pass over all the rest, at what
price do you reckon it, that, had I not been your devoted
and dedicated client, your wife would still be a virgin?
You know well, surely, in what ways, how often you begged this of me,
and what you promised: the fleeing girl I often
seized in my embrace; she had even torn up the contract and was now
re-signing: this I scarcely redeemed in a whole night
while you wept outside; the little bed is my witness, and you,
to whom the sound of the couch and the mistress's voice came through.
A marriage unstable, begun to break up, and now almost dissolved,
the adulterer has saved in many a house.
Which way will you turn? What will you set down first, what last?
Is it nothing, then, ungrateful and treacherous one, nothing,
that a little son or a daughter is born to you from me?
For you acknowledge them, and love to scatter through the public records
the proofs of your manhood. Hang garlands on your doors:
now you are a father; I have given you what you may set against gossip;
you have a parent's rights; thanks to me you are written down an heir,
you take whole legacies, and the sweet windfall too.
And many advantages besides will be added to the windfalls,
if I complete the number, if I make it three." Just is the cause
of your grief, Naevolus; but what does he bring against it?
"He neglects me and seeks himself another two-legged donkey.
Remember to keep these things, entrusted to you alone, hidden,
and silently lock my complaints within yourself.
For it is deadly to have an enemy smooth with pumice;
he who lately shared a secret burns and hates,
as if I had betrayed all I know. He does not hesitate to take up
steel, to open a head with a club, to set a candle to the doors;
nor are you to scorn or despise the fact that,
with these riches, poison is never dear.
So keep my secrets hidden as the court of Mars at Athens."
O Corydon, Corydon, do you think any secret of a rich man's
can stay hidden? Though the slaves keep silent, the beasts will speak,
and the dog and the doorposts and the marble. Close the windows,
let curtains cover the chinks, fasten the doors, take away the light,
drive everyone out of the way, let no one lie near:
yet what he does at the second cock-crow,
the nearest tavern-keeper will know before daybreak, and will hear what
the confectioner and the head-cooks' carvers
have invented alike. For what crime do they scruple to frame
against their masters, as often as they avenge with rumors
their floggings? Nor will one be lacking to seek you through the crossroads
against your will, and drunkenly soak your wretched ear.
So beg of them what you were lately asking
of us: that they keep silent. But they would rather betray
a secret than drink the stolen Falernian,
doing for the people as much as Saufeia used to drink.
One should live uprightly for many reasons, but chiefly
for these: that you may scorn the tongues of your slaves,
for the tongue is the worst part of a bad slave;
yet worse is he who is not free of those
whose lives he keeps with his own grain and money.
"You have given useful counsel just now, but a commonplace one;
what do you advise me now, after my loss of time and my deceived
hopes? For the little flower of our narrow and wretched life
hastens to run swiftly down to its briefest
portion; while we drink, while we call for garlands, perfumes, girls,
old age creeps up unperceived."
Never fear; you will never lack a pathic friend
while these hills stand safe and sound: from everywhere to them
will gather, by carriage and by ship, all
who scratch their head with one finger. A still greater
hope remains for you: only set your tooth to the rocket-salad.
"Keep these counsels for the fortunate; but my Clotho
and my Lachesis are content, if the belly is fed through the groin.
O my little household gods, whom with a grain of incense
or meal and a slender garland I am wont to entreat,
when shall I fix on something to make my old age safe
from the beggar's mat and the staff? Twenty thousand in interest
on pledges laid down, some little vessels of plain silver—
but such as the censor Fabricius would mark down—and two stout
fellows from the Moesian herd, who, with their necks lent me,
may bid me stand secure in the clamorous circus;
let me have besides a stooping engraver, and another
who paints many faces quickly: these are enough,
since I shall be poor. A pitiable wish, and no hope
even of this; for when Fortune is invoked on my behalf,
she has stopped her ears with the wax fetched from that ship
which escaped the Sicilian songs with its deafened oarsman."

Satire X In all the lands that stretch from Cadiz to the dawn and to the Ganges, few can tell true goods from their reverse, once the fog of error is dispersed. For what do we, by reason, fear or crave? What plan do you conceive so blessed in its start that you do not repent the effort and the prayer fulfilled? Whole houses the obliging gods have overthrown at the owners' own asking. In civil life and in the camp alike we ask for things that ruin us. To many their own rushing flood of eloquence is deadly; another trusted in his strength and his astonishing arms, and died. But more are throttled by money piled up with too much care, and by a fortune that outdoes all patrimonies as far as a British whale outdoes the dolphins. So in the dreadful days, at Nero's command, a whole cohort shut up Longinus and the vast gardens of the over-rich Seneca, and besieged the noble halls of the Laterani: rarely does the soldier climb to a garret. Though you carry but a few small cups of plain silver by night, you will be afraid of the sword and the spear, you will tremble at the shadow of a reed stirred in the moonlight; the empty-handed traveller will sing in the robber's face. The first and best-known prayer, in every temple, is for riches: that our wealth may grow, that ours may be the largest strongbox in the whole Forum. But no poison is drunk from earthenware: fear it when you take up a jewelled cup, and the Setine wine glows in broad gold. Do you not now approve, then, that of the two sages, one would laugh each time he had moved a single foot across the threshold, while the other, opposite, would weep? But the censure of harsh laughter comes easily to anyone: the wonder is where the other found enough moisture for his eyes. Democritus would shake his lungs with endless laughter, though in those cities of his there were no purple-bordered robes, no rods of office, no litter, no tribunal. What if he had seen the praetor towering high upon his lofty car, raised in the dust of the mid circus, in Jove's own tunic, bearing on his shoulders the Tyrian embroidered hangings of his painted toga, and the great crown's vast circle, too wide for any neck? For a public slave holds it, sweating, and—lest the consul grow too pleased with himself—that slave rides in the same car. Add now the bird that rises on the ivory sceptre, the horn-blowers on this side, on that the long line marching before him in attendance, and the white-robed citizens at his bridle, friends made his own by the dole stowed deep in their purses. Even then Democritus found matter for laughter at every meeting of men: his wisdom shows that the greatest men, who will give great examples, can be born in a land of dolts under a thick, dull sky. He laughed at the cares and likewise at the joys of the crowd, and at times their tears, while to Fortune herself, when she threatened, he would offer the noose and show her the middle finger. So the things we ask for are superfluous or ruinous, those for which it is right to wax the knees of the gods! Some men a power perched too high casts down to envy's ruin; the long and splendid roll of their honours sinks them; down come the statues, dragged along by the rope, then the axe driven into the very wheels of the chariots hacks them, and the legs of the undeserving horses are broken. Now the fires hiss, now in the bellows and the furnaces the head once worshipped by the people glows, and the great Sejanus crackles; then from the face that ranked second in all the world are made jugs, basins, a frying-pan, chamber-pots. Hang up the laurel at your door, lead to the Capitol a great chalked ox! Sejanus is dragged along by the hook, a sight for all; everyone rejoices: "What lips, what a face the man had! Never—if you believe me—did I love this fellow. But on what charge did he fall? Who was the informer? On whose evidence, by what witness, was it proved?" "Nothing of the sort: a long and wordy letter came from Capri." "Quite right—I ask no more." But what does the rabble of Remus do? It follows fortune, as always, and hates the condemned. That same people, had Nortia favoured her Etruscan, had the old emperor been struck down unawares, would this very hour be hailing Sejanus as Augustus. Long since—from the time we sold our votes to no one—it has shed its cares; for the people that once handed out command, the rods, legions, everything, now holds itself in check, and anxiously longs for two things only: bread and the games. "I hear many will perish." "No doubt—the furnace is big." "My poor pale friend Brutidius met me by the altar of Mars; how I fear that the beaten Ajax may exact a penalty, as if defended badly." "Let us run headlong, and while he lies on the bank, trample Caesar's enemy." "But let the slaves look on, lest one of them deny it and drag his terrified master, neck noosed, to judgment." Such was the talk then about Sejanus, these the secret mutterings of the crowd. Would you like to be greeted as Sejanus was, to hold as much, to bestow on this man the highest curule chairs, to set that man over armies, to be reckoned guardian of an emperor who sits on the narrow crag of Capri amid his herd of Chaldaeans? You would surely want the javelins, the cohorts, the splendid knights, and a camp of your own; and why not crave these things? Even men who would kill no one want the power to. But what glory and success is worth so much, that the measure of evils should match the measure of joys? Would you rather take up the bordered robe of this man dragged along, or hold authority over Fidenae and Gabii, and lay down the law over weights, breaking undersized measures, a ragged aedile in deserted Ulubrae? So you admit you did not know what was to be wished: for he who craved excessive honours and demanded excessive wealth was piling up the many storeys of a lofty tower, from which the fall would be the higher, the sheer plunge of the toppled ruin the more vast. What overthrew the Crassi, the Pompeys, and the man who broke the Romans and led them tamed to his own lash? The topmost place, sought of course by every art, and great prayers granted by the malignant gods. Few kings go down to Ceres' son-in-law without slaughter and wound, few tyrants by a bloodless death. Eloquence and the fame of Demosthenes or Cicero each man begins to long for, and longs for through the whole festival, whoever still worships at his thrifty penny's Minerva, attended by a slave to guard his little satchel. Yet by his eloquence each orator perished; the rich and overflowing fountain of his genius gave each to death. For his genius the hand and neck of one was cut off; never did the Rostra drip with the blood of a petty pleader. "O fortunate Rome, born in my consulship!" He could have scorned Antony's swords, had he spoken all his speeches thus. I would rather have his laughable verses than you, divine Philippic of conspicuous fame, unrolling next after the first. And that man too—a savage end snatched him away, whom Athens marvelled at, as he poured forth his torrent and governed the reins of the crowded theatre. He was born under hostile gods, an ill-starred fate, the man whose father, blear-eyed from the soot of the glowing ore, sent him from the coal and the tongs and the forge that fashions swords and from the grimy Vulcan—to a teacher of rhetoric. The spoils of war—a breastplate fixed to a mutilated trophy, a cheek-piece hanging from a broken helmet, a yoke shorn of its pole, the flagstaff of a beaten trireme, and a sad captive on the arch's top— these are believed greater than human goods. To this the Roman, the Greek, the barbarian general has roused himself; for this he had his reasons for danger and toil. So much greater is the thirst for fame than for virtue: for who would embrace virtue herself, if you took away the rewards? Yet long ago the glory of a few brought ruin on their country, and the lust for praise and the title that will cling to the stones that guard their ashes—stones that the worthless strength of a barren fig-tree can shatter, since to the very tombs a fate is given. Weigh Hannibal: how many pounds will you find in that supreme commander? This is the man whom Africa cannot hold, beaten by the Moorish ocean and stretched toward the warm Nile, then back again to the Ethiopian peoples and other elephants! Spain is added to his empire; the Pyrenees he leaps across. Nature set against him the Alps and the snow: he splits the rocks and bursts the mountain with vinegar. Now he holds Italy, yet still he strives to push beyond: "Nothing is done," he says, "until with Punic soldiery I break the gates and plant my standard in the heart of the Subura." O what a face, and worthy of what a portrait, when the Gaetulian beast bore the one-eyed general! What, then, is his end? O glory! That same man is conquered, flees headlong into exile, and there, a great and wondered-at client, sits at a king's palace gate, until it please the Bithynian tyrant to wake. The end of that soul, which once threw human affairs into turmoil, no sword shall give, no stones, no spears—but that avenger of Cannae, that requiter of so much blood, a ring. Go, madman, race across the savage Alps, to please schoolboys and become a theme for declamation! One world is not enough for the youth of Pella; the unhappy man frets at the narrow bounds of the world, as though shut up on the crags of Gyara or tiny Seriphos; yet when he enters the city walled by the potters, a sarcophagus will content him. Death alone confesses how small are the bodies of men. Athos, they say, was once sailed through—whatever lying Greece dares in her histories—and the solid sea was bridged with those same fleets and set beneath the wheels; we believe that deep rivers ran dry, and that the streams were drunk up by the Mede at his breakfast, and all that Sostratus sings of with his dripping wings. Yet how did that man return, after Salamis was left behind— he who was wont to rage with whips against the North-West and the East wind, which never suffered such things in their Aeolian prison, who had bound Earth-Shaker himself with fetters? A mild stroke, surely, that he did not also think the god worth branding! Who of the gods would consent to serve such a master? But how did he come back? In a single ship, indeed, through bloody waves, the prow slow through dense corpses. Such penalties did the glory so often longed-for exact. "Grant length of life, grant many years, O Jupiter": this, with steady face, this alone you pray, and even pale you pray it. But with how unbroken and how great a train of ills is long old age beset! First, look at the face, deformed and hideous and unlike its former self, the ugly hide instead of skin, the sagging cheeks, and wrinkles such as, where Thabraca spreads her shaded glades, an aged mother ape scratches on her withered jowl. Among the young there are many differences: one is handsomer than this, and that than another, one far stronger than the next. But the old have one face: limbs that tremble with the voice, a head now bald, the dripping infancy of a runny nose; the wretch must crumble his bread with toothless gums; so burdensome is he to wife and children and himself that he would stir disgust even in the legacy-hunter Cossus. His dulled palate finds no longer the same joy in wine and food; sex is long since forgotten, or if you try, the small, ruptured member lies still, and though caressed all night, will still lie still. What can it hope for, this grey hair of a sick groin? And is not lust rightly suspect that strives for love without the strength for it? Now look at the loss of another faculty. For what pleasure is there in a singer, be he ever so fine, in a lyre-player or a Seleucus, in those whose custom it is to shine in a gilded cloak? What does it matter in which part of the great theatre he sits, who can scarcely hear the horn-blowers and the blare of the trumpets in concert? A shout is needed for his ear to catch what the boy announces—who has come, what hour it is. Besides, the scant blood now in his chilled body is warm with fever alone; in close array there leap about him every kind of disease, whose names if you should ask, I could sooner reckon up how many adulterers Oppia has loved, how many patients Themison killed in one autumn, how many partners Basilus, how many wards Hirrus has cheated, how many men long Maura drains dry in a single day, how many pupils Hamillus corrupts; I could run through more quickly how many country-houses he owns now under whose shears my heavy beard once rasped as a youth. One is weak in the shoulder, this in the loins, this in the hip; another has lost both his eyes, and envies the one-eyed; this man's pale lips take their food from another's fingers, and he who used at the mere sight of dinner to open wide his jaws now only gapes, like a young swallow to which the fasting mother flies with full mouth. But worse than every loss of limb is the madness that recognizes neither the names of slaves nor the face of the friend with whom he dined the night before, nor those he begot, those he reared. For by a cruel will he forbids his own to be his heirs; the whole estate is carried off to Phiale: so much avails the breath of that practised mouth that stood for many years in the brothel's prison-cell. Though the powers of his mind stay vigorous, still he must lead the funerals of his sons, must look upon the pyre of his beloved wife, and of his brother, and the urns full of sisters. This is the penalty of long life: that, with the household's calamity forever renewed, a man should grow old in many griefs and in unending mourning and in black attire. The king of Pylos—if you give Homer any credit— was a model of a life second only to the crow's, happy no doubt, who through so many ages put off death and now reckons his years on his right hand, and so often drank the new wine. But I beg you, listen a little to how he himself complains of the laws of the Fates and of the over-long thread, when he sees keen Antilochus' beard ablaze, and asks of every comrade present why he has lasted into these times, what crime he has committed to deserve so long an age. This same lament Peleus makes, mourning Achilles snatched away, and another, whose right it is to mourn the Ithacan as he swims. With Troy still standing, Priam might have come to the shades of Assaracus in great solemnity, with Hector bearing his bier, and the rest of his brothers' shoulders, amid the tears of the women of Ilium, while Cassandra began the first wailing, and Polyxena with her robe torn, if he had died at another time, before Paris began to build his reckless ships. What, then, did length of days bring him? He saw everything overthrown, and Asia falling to flame and sword. Then, a trembling soldier, he laid aside his crown, took up arms, and fell before the altar of highest Jove, like an old ox, which offers to its master's knife a thin and pitiful neck, scorned now by the ungrateful plough. That, however it was, was a man's end; but with a dog's snarling jaws his wife, who lived on after him, gave tongue. I hasten to our own, and pass over the king of Pontus and Croesus, whom the eloquent voice of just Solon bade look to the final span of a long life. Exile, prison, the marshes of Minturnae, and bread begged at conquered Carthage— from this length of days these things had their cause. What, of that citizen, could Nature have brought forth on earth, what more blessed could Rome ever have had, if, with the captives' column led about him and all the pomp of war, he had breathed out his rich soul, when he was about to step down from the Teutonic car? Provident Campania had given Pompey fevers much to be wished for; but the many cities and the public prayers prevailed: so the Fortune of himself and of the city took off, preserved for defeat, his head. This torture Lentulus escaped, this penalty Cethegus, and fell whole, and Catiline lay a corpse entire. The anxious mother prays in a low voice for beauty in her boys, in a louder for her girls, when she sees Venus' shrine, right up to extravagance of vows. "But why," she says, "would you reproach me? Latona delights in fair Diana." Yet Lucretia forbids the praying for a face such as she herself had; Verginia would long to take on Rutila's hump and give Rutila her own. Yet a son of outstanding body keeps his parents wretched and afraid forever; so rare is the harmony of beauty and chastity. Though a stern household, in imitation of the old Sabines, has handed down holy ways to him, and though kindly Nature, with a lavish hand, has granted him a chaste disposition and a face that flushes with modest blood—what more can she give a boy than a guardian, and one mightier than any?—still he is not allowed to be a man; for the prodigal shamelessness of the corrupter dares to tempt the very parents: so great is their trust in their bribes. No tyrant ever castrated an ugly youth in his cruel castle, nor did Nero ever carry off a boy who was club-footed or scrofulous or swollen alike with belly and with hump. Go now and take joy in your son's good looks, for whom greater perils wait: he will become a public adulterer, and dread all the penalties that the law of a husband's anger owes; nor will he be luckier than the star of Mars, so as never to fall into the snares. And sometimes that wrath exacts more than any law has granted to wrath: one kills with the sword, another slashes with bloody whips; into some adulterers even the mullet enters. But your Endymion will become the lover of a beloved matron; soon, when Servilia gives him money, he will become hers too whom he does not love, and will strip off all her body's adornment: for what would any woman refuse to her wet loins, whether it be this Oppia or Catulla? The whole character of the woman lies there. "But how does beauty harm the chaste?" Why, what did his stern resolve profit Hippolytus, what Bellerophon? Each woman flushed, as if scorned, at the rebuff, and Stheneboea blazed no less than the Cretan, and both worked themselves to fury: a woman is at her most savage when shame goads her hatred. Now choose what counsel you think should be given to the man whom Caesar's wife is set on marrying. The best of men, and the most handsome too, of a patrician house, is being hauled off, poor wretch, to be undone by Messalina's eyes. She has long been sitting, the bridal veil made ready, the Tyrian marriage-couch spread openly in the gardens, and a million in the old style is to be given, the augur will come with the men who seal the contract. Did you think these things secret, entrusted to a few? She will not marry except in lawful form. Say, what is your choice? If you will not obey, you must die before the lamps are lit; if you commit the crime, a little respite will be given, while the matter, known to city and people, reaches the emperor's ear: last of all will he learn his house's disgrace. Meanwhile obey the command, if a few days of life are worth so much. Whatever you think the lighter or the better course, that fair white neck must be offered to the sword. Shall men then ask for nothing? If you want my counsel, you will let the gods themselves decide what suits us and what is useful for our affairs; for in place of pleasant things the gods will give what is most fitting. Man is dearer to them than to himself. We, driven by the impulse of our hearts and by blind and mighty desire, ask for marriage and for offspring from a wife; but to them it is known what the children, what the wife, will turn out to be. Still, that you may ask something and offer at the shrines the entrails and the divine sausages of a little white pig, you should pray for a sound mind in a sound body. Ask for a brave heart that has no fear of death, that counts the last span of life among the gifts of Nature, that can bear whatever toils, that knows no anger, craves nothing, and holds the labours and savage tasks of Hercules better than the loves and the feasts and the down-pillow of Sardanapalus. What I show you, you can give yourself: the one path to a tranquil life lies surely open through virtue. You have no divine power, Fortune, if there is wisdom: it is we, we who make you a goddess and set you in heaven.

Satire XI If Atticus dines lavishly, he is called a man of taste; if Rutilus does, a madman. For what raises a louder laugh in the crowd than a poor Apicius? Every dinner-party, the baths, the lounging-places, every theatre, is full of Rutilus; for while his strong and youthful limbs are equal to the helmet, and while they burn with blood, he means— not, indeed, that the tribune forces him, but neither does he forbid it— to sign the trainer's terms and the words a gladiator swears. And you see many more whom their oft-tricked creditor is wont to wait for at the very entrance of the meat-market, men whose one reason for living lies in their palate. The most wretched of them dines the most exquisitely, and the best, he who is soon to fall, his ruin already showing through. Meanwhile they hunt for delicacies through all the elements, with no price ever standing in their appetite's way; look closer, and the things that please them more are the ones that cost the more. So it is no hard thing to raise a sum that must be lost by pawning the plate, or by breaking a mother's likeness, and to season a gluttonous dish with four hundred sesterces; thus they come to the gladiator-school's hash. It matters, then, who prepares these same dishes: in Rutilus it is luxury, in Ventidius it takes a praiseworthy name, and draws its fame from his fortune. That man I shall justly despise, who knows how much higher Atlas towers than all the mountains in Libya, yet this same man is ignorant how far the iron-bound strongbox stands from the little money-bag. From heaven came down "Know thyself," to be fixed and pondered in a mindful heart, whether you seek a marriage, or wish to hold a seat in the sacred senate; for Thersites does not demand Achilles' breastplate, in which Ulysses made himself a laughing-stock. If you set about defending a doubtful case at great risk, take counsel of yourself, tell yourself who you are, a forceful orator, or a Curtius and a windbag Matho. A man must know his own measure and keep it in view in matters great and small alike, even when a fish is to be bought: do not crave a mullet when there is only a gudgeon in your purse. For what end awaits you, your purse failing and your gullet swelling, with a father's money and your whole estate sunk into a belly that can hold the weight of usury and silver, of flocks and fields? From such masters last of all, after everything, departs the ring, and Pollio begs with a naked finger. It is not the early ashes nor the untimely funeral that luxury need fear, but old age, more to be dreaded than death. These are mostly the steps: money is borrowed at Rome and spent before the lenders' eyes; then when a little something or other is left, and the moneylender grows pale, they who would change their soil run off to Baiae and the oyster-beds. For to flee the Forum is now no worse a thing than to move from the seething Subura to the Esquiline; the only grief, the only sorrow for those fleeing their country, is to have missed the games for a single year. Not a drop of blood stays in their cheek; few stay to mock at modesty as it flees the city. You shall find out today, Persicus, whether all these fine words I fail to make good by my life, my conduct, my deeds— whether, praising lentils, I am a secret glutton, and order porridge aloud before others, but cakes in the boy's ear. For since you are my promised guest, you will find an Evander in me; you will come as a Tirynthian, or as a guest lesser than he, yet himself too touching heaven by blood, the one sent to the stars by water, the other by fire. Now hear my courses, furnished by no markets. From my Tiburtine farm will come a fattest kid, the tenderest of the whole flock, that knows no grass and has never dared to nibble the twigs of the low willow, that has more milk in him than blood; and mountain asparagus, gathered by the bailiff's wife when her spindle was laid by; besides, great eggs still warm in their twisted hay are here, along with the very hens that laid them; and grapes kept for part of the year, just as they hung on the vines, Signian and Syrian pears, and from the same baskets apples that rival the Picene and smell of fresh fragrance, nor are they to be feared by you, since the cold has dried away their autumn and laid to rest the dangers of unripe juice. This was once a luxurious dinner for our senate; Curius, with his own hands, would set on his small hearth the few greens he had picked in his little garden—greens which now a filthy ditch-digger disdains in his heavy chains, who remembers the taste of a sow's paunch from the hot cook-shop. It was once the custom, on feast-days, to keep the back of a dried pig hanging on an open rack, and to set out the birthday bacon to one's kinsmen, adding fresh meat, if some sacrifice had supplied it. Some kinsman who had borne the title of three times consul, the commands of camps, the honour of dictator, would come to such a feast earlier than was his wont, bringing back his mattock from the hill he had subdued. But when men trembled before the Fabii and stern Cato, before the Scauri and Fabricius, when even his own colleague feared the harsh and rigid censor's ways, no one counted it among his cares and serious concerns what kind of turtle swam in the swell of Ocean, to make a bright and noble headboard for the sons of Troy; but the bronze front of their small couches, with bare sides, showed the cheap head of an ass with a garland on it, about which the children of the playful countryside would frolic: such food, then, as the house and furniture. At that time, rough and unable to admire Greek arts, the soldier, finding among his share of plunder from sacked cities the cups of great craftsmen, would break them up, so that his horse might delight in trappings, and his chased helmet might show to the enemy doomed to die the image of the She-wolf of Rome, tamed by the empire's destiny, of the twin sons of Quirinus under the crag, and the naked figure of the god, advancing with shield and spear, poised in air. They set their spelt-porridge, then, in a Tuscan dish: what silver there was shone on their arms alone. Everything then was such that you would envy it, if you were of an envious bent. The majesty of the temples too was nearer at hand, and a voice heard near midnight, through the middle of the city, when the Gauls were coming from the shore of Ocean and the gods were doing the office of prophet, warned us of these things. Such was the care that he was wont to give to the affairs of Latium, that Jupiter of clay, undefiled by any gold. Those times saw tables born at home, made from our own tree; for this use the wood would stand ready, if perchance the East wind had brought down an aged walnut. But now the rich have no pleasure in dining, no taste in the turbot, in the venison; the perfumes and the roses seem to stink, unless broad table-tops are upheld by great ivory, by a tall leopard with wide-gaping jaws, made from those tusks that the gate of Syene sends, and the swift Moors, and the Indian darker than the Moor, and those that the beast has shed in the Nabataean glade, now grown too large and heavy for its head. From this rises the appetite, from this comes strength to the stomach; for to them a silver foot is what an iron ring is on the finger.
